isBasedOn.name: UK Data and AI Ethics Framework

@graph.name: Overview
@graph.marin:text: Data is information we collect and record, such as a count, a date, or a status. Government uses data to see what people need, run services well, and explain its choices. Good data is accurate, current, and easy to find. It is also handled with care and shared under clear rules. You do not need to be a data expert. You do need to ask good questions about the data behind a decision.

@graph.name: Why it matters
marin:items: Data shows what people need, so services can match real needs.
Poor-quality data leads to weak decisions.
Clear rules for sharing data help teams work together and avoid delays.
The public trusts government more when it explains how it uses data.
Careful use of data protects privacy and prevents harm.

@graph.name: Problem
@graph.marin:text: Many teams cannot find, trust, or share the data they need. Records are incomplete or out of date, and owners are unclear. Leaders then decide with weak evidence, and the public has little reason to trust the result.

@graph.name: Solution
@graph.marin:text: Treat data as a shared asset. Name an owner for each data set. Check its quality and say plainly what it can and cannot do. Share it under clear rules, protect personal information, and tell the public how you use it.

@graph.name: User stories
marin:items: As a department head, I want to know if our data is good, so I can trust my decisions.
As a program manager, I want to find data other teams hold, so I do not start over.
As an analyst, I want clear sharing rules, so I can answer requests fast.
As a resident, I want to know how the County uses my information, so I can trust it.

marin:items.definition: How well data fits its use. It can be complete, unique, consistent, timely, valid, and accurate.
All expected records are there, and the key values are filled in.
The data matches what is true in the real world.
The data is up to date when you need it.
An agreed way to name, format, and describe data so it can be shared and combined.
Clear roles, rules, and accountability for how data is managed and used.
The person responsible for a set of data and who can use it.
Details that describe data, such as what it means, where it came from, and known issues.
A written deal on what data is shared, why, and how it is protected.

marin:items.do: Ask who owns the data and how current it is.
marin:items.dont: Use numbers without knowing where they came from.

marin:items.do: Say plainly how good the data is and what it can be used for.
marin:items.dont: Hide known gaps or errors in the data.

marin:items.do: Bring in privacy and legal staff early when sharing data.
marin:items.dont: Share personal data first and check the rules later.

marin:items.do: Collect only the data you need for a clear purpose.
marin:items.dont: Keep data just in case it might be useful.

marin:items.do: Use common standards so data can be combined.
marin:items.dont: Create a new data format for every project.

marin:items.do: Tell the public why you collect data and how you use it.
marin:items.dont: Assume people know how their data is used.

@graph.name: Questions to ask
marin:items: What decision will this data help us make?
Who owns this data, and who can answer questions about it?
How complete, accurate, and up to date is it?
What is missing, and who might be left out?
Does it include personal information, and are we allowed to use it?
Who else might need this data, and how can they ask for it?
How will we explain our use of this data to the public?

@graph.name: Checklist
marin:items: I can say what decision the data supports.
I know who owns the data.
I checked that the data is complete, accurate, and current.
I know the limits of the data and can explain them in plain words.
Privacy and legal staff have reviewed any personal data.
I collected only the data I need.
Others can find the data and know how to ask for it.

@graph.name: Mantras
marin:items: Know the source.
Say how good the data is.
Collect only what you need.
Share under clear rules.
Explain it in plain words.
